text.kicker: Even under ice in a Churchill winter, light is a resource. Algae photosynthesise with chlorophyll in their plastids. Many heterotrophic bacteria top up their energy with light as well, either with bacteriochlorophyll reaction centres (aerobic anoxygenic photosynthesis, AAP, typical of roseobacters) or with rhodopsin proton pumps. This page follows 17 light-gene groups through both winters against a modelled light curve. No light was measured, so the model gives the clear-sky maximum above the ice. Expression is CPM of protein-coding reads, with hosts from MAGs or, for unbinned contigs, Kaiju; claims about regulation use each genome’s own transcripts. One pool per treatment, so all contrasts are descriptive.

text.sky: Churchill (58.8° N) never has polar night: on the winter solstice the sun is up for 5.9 hours and reaches about 8° above the horizon. The model gives clear-sky daily PAR from 2.5 mol photons m⁻² d⁻¹ at the solstice to about 13 by mid-February, a roughly 5-fold rise over each experiment. Both experiments start near the darkest point, so every sample series also runs along a rising light curve. The coloured curves estimate how much of it reached the water under each pool’s snow and ice.
text.underice: Under the ice, a simple model (no roof, cloud or oil) attenuates the clear-sky light by each pool’s measured snow and ice: transmitted fraction = (1 − albedo) × exp(−15 m⁻¹ × snow − 1.5 m⁻¹ × ice), with albedo 0.85 for snow, 0.50 for bare ice and 0.07 for open water. In 2025-26 both pools start nearly open (up to 90% of surface light transmitted in the diesel pool, 43% in the control), then fall to about 1% once snow settles on 30–80 cm of ice after about day 20, so the water darkens even as daylight returns. In 2024-25 the cores start at about 20 cm of ice with a little snow, so only 2%–8% gets through all season. Snow and ice are interpolated between core days and held flat before the first core. Under-ice light is not just a calendar: it drops sharply when snow settles, and in 2025-26 the pools differ. Season itself is not a cause; microbes feel it through light, temperature, ice growth, brine and nutrients, which all change together, so raw correlations with under-ice light are seasonal signals that light may or may not drive. A stricter test asks whether light explains anything beyond the shared seasonal trajectory, by removing a linear time trend within each pool. Nothing passes it: across the 17 gene groups the smallest q is 0.07, and across 182 within-genome light-gene shares the smallest q is 0.09 (median partial r −0.04 for AAP, +0.10 for rhodopsins and −0.19 for plastid photosynthesis in 2025-26). That does not rule light out; it means light cannot be separated from the other seasonal drivers with one pool per treatment. One raw correlation is clearly not light: plastid photosystems against under-ice light in the 2025-26 diesel pool (r about +0.8) is the diesel-driven algal collapse happening while the ice thickened. Vertical lines mark the logged roof state on 2025-26 sampling days (solid = open, dotted = closed); it was not logged in 2024-25.
text.algae: Plastid photosynthesis transcripts collapse in the 2025-26 diesel pool (photosystem II −3.5 log₂, BACI −3.3). That is the algal loss shown on the Eukaryotes page: plastid MAGs fall to 10,122 TPM in diesel-pool water against 38,791 in the control (both pools 44,258–53,274 before dosing). Within the plastids, though, the share of transcripts that are photosynthesis genes does not change: 801‰ in the diesel pool vs 766‰ in the control after dosing. Across 16 plastid and cyanobacterial genomes, the within-genome BACI is 0.0. The surviving algae are not visibly shaded or switched off, at the level of plastid transcription. Photosynthesis genes are lower in top ice than bottom ice (2 of 13 pairs higher at the top), as expected for bottom-ice algae.
text.genomes: Community AAP transcripts rise with diesel because AAP roseobacters, mainly Sulfitobacter, are more abundant in the diesel pool. Within each genome the AAP share does not rise: median within-genome BACI −0.62 (2 of 9 genomes up). Rhodopsins are flat as well (−0.09, 12 of 29 up). So diesel did not make the heterotrophs lean harder on light. Correlations with modelled PAR inside each pool are near zero (median r −0.1 to +0.1), so no seasonal switch-on shows up either. Most AAP and rhodopsin genomes express less of their light genes in ice than in the water below.
text.partition: AAP is almost entirely alphaproteobacterial (77% of reaction-centre transcripts; roseobacters such as Sulfitobacter, Octadecabacter, Planktomarina and RS62), with gammaproteobacteria at 13%. Proton-pumping rhodopsins are spread more widely: alphaproteobacteria 36% (mostly SAR11-type), actinobacteria 30%, Bacteroidota 17%. Rhodopsins carry about ten times as many transcripts as AAP reaction centres overall.
text.m1122: On the Physiological states page this Sulfitobacter’s water state loads PufH next to the ammonium transporter. The AAP share confirms it: AAP genes are 5.9‰ of its transcripts in water against 2.7‰ in ice (Mann–Whitney p < 0.0001). Within seawater, AAP share runs with the nitrogen-hungry end of PC1 (Spearman r +0.59 with PC1) and with its own nitrogen-acquisition share (r +0.33). Against the under-ice light model it runs the other way: in 2025-26 water the AAP share falls as modelled under-ice light rises (r −0.68 in the diesel pool, −0.44 in the control) and climbs as snow and ice thicken through the season (r with day +0.71). It does not follow surface daylight, which returns over the same weeks (r +0.02 diesel, −0.14 control). So the seasonal cue it tracks is the darkening water, or something else that changes with the season (ice growth, brine drainage, nitrogen drawdown), not returning daylight. Making more light-harvesting machinery in dim light is how roseobacter AAP is regulated, so darkening is a plausible driver. With experiment day held constant the correlation is +0.01: the AAP rise follows the seasonal trajectory, with no extra light signal on top of it.
reading: Observed: diesel removed algae, not their photosynthesis. Plastid photosystem transcripts fall about 11× in 2025-26 diesel seawater, in step with plastid abundance. The surviving plastids keep the same photosynthesis share (801 vs 766‰). Shading by oil, if any, does not show in plastid transcription.

Observed: light effects cannot be separated from season. Light genes change through the winter, but no gene group or genome follows modelled under-ice light beyond the shared seasonal trajectory (no q < 0.05 after removing a within-pool time trend). Light, temperature, ice growth and nutrients all change together. Light-harvesting bacteria did not switch on with diesel either. AAP transcripts rise (+2.2 log₂) only because roseobacters bloom; within genomes AAP and rhodopsin shares are flat (BACI −0.62 and −0.09). Light is not obviously used as a stress subsidy here.

Observed: the top of the ice senses light. BLUF blue-light photoreceptors (13/13 pairs), PpsR/AppA (the light- and redox-sensing repressor of AAP genes; 12/13) and photolyases (12/13) are higher in top ice than bottom ice. This fits more light, and more UV damage to repair, near the ice surface. Composition differs between layers, so this is not a within-genome result.

Observed, in one genome: AAP rises as the water darkens and nitrogen runs short. Sulfitobacter metabat_1122 expresses more AAP genes in water than in ice and most in its nitrogen-hungry state. Through 2025-26 its AAP share climbs as modelled under-ice light falls, not as surface daylight returns. Dim-light induction of AAP fits; nitrogen drawdown and ice growth move over the same weeks and remain alternatives.

Model caveat. Surface PAR is a clear-sky maximum above the ice (Haurwitz irradiance; PAR = 0.45 × GHI; 4.57 µmol J⁻¹). It rises steadily through both experiments, so it is confounded with experiment day; correlations with it can only be called consistent with seasonal light return. The under-ice curve adds measured snow and ice but uses textbook attenuation values and ignores the roof, cloud and oil; under-ice PAR sensors in each pool would make light a usable covariate.
